caption: Each body drawn on its own, with only its own forces: the same T and the same a.

md: A light inextensible string over a smooth pulley carries the same pull at both ends, and it stops either body moving without the other. Those two facts make a pair of bodies solvable.

Draw each body on its own with only its own forces, using the **same $T$** and the **same $a$** for both. Write one equation for each, in that body's own direction of travel, and **add them**: the $T$ terms cancel, leaving one equation in $a$.

stem: Blocks of 9 kg and 6 kg hang either side of a smooth pulley and are released. Find their acceleration and the tension in the string. Take $g = 10$ m/s².

steps.decision: The heavier block goes down, so its weight comes first and the tension holds it back.
The lighter block goes up: the tension lifts it and its weight holds it back. The same $T$, the same $a$.
The $T$ terms cancel. Both masses stay on the right, because both blocks accelerate.
Put $a$ back into either equation, then check in the other: $90 - 72 = 18$, which is $9 \times 2$.

prompt: Blocks of 7 kg and 3 kg hang either side of a smooth pulley and are released. What is their acceleration, in m/s²? Take $g = 10$ m/s².
explain: As in steps 1 to 3 of See it: $70 - T = 7a$ and $T - 30 = 3a$ add to $40 = 10a$, so $a = 4$ m/s². Both masses go on the right, because both blocks accelerate.

twin.prompt: Blocks of 16 kg and 4 kg hang either side of a smooth pulley and are released. What is their acceleration, in m/s²? Take $g = 10$ m/s².

text: Why one tension and one acceleration

md: A light string has no mass, so the pull at one end equals the pull at the other, and a smooth pulley passes it on unchanged: one letter, $T$, for both bodies. An inextensible string cannot stretch, so when one body moves 1 cm the other moves 1 cm too: one acceleration, $a$.

title: Why adding removes T
md: The string pulls each body towards the pulley. In one body's equation $T$ helps the motion; in the other's it opposes it.

stem: The 9 kg and 6 kg blocks above: show why adding their equations of motion removes the tension.

steps.decision: The string pulls this block up, against its motion, so $T$ enters with a minus sign.
The same string pulls this block up too, the way it moves, so $T$ enters with a plus sign.
One string, one tension: it helps one motion exactly as much as it opposes the other, so the pair cancel.

prompt: Two connected bodies each have an equation of motion. Why do the tension terms cancel when the two equations are added?
options: T helps one body's motion and opposes the other's
The tension is zero while the bodies accelerate
The two bodies have equal weights
answer: T helps one body's motion and opposes the other's
explain: The same pull acts along the string on both bodies, against one body's motion and with the other's, as steps 1 and 2 of See it show: $-T$ and $+T$. So they cancel. The tension is not zero: it is still there in each equation.

twin.prompt: A car tows a trailer by a tow-bar. Why does the tension not appear in the equation for the car and trailer together?
options: It pulls the trailer forwards and the car backwards, so it cancels
The tension is zero while they accelerate
The trailer is lighter than the car
twin.answer: It pulls the trailer forwards and the car backwards, so it cancels
twin.explain: The tow-bar pulls both vehicles equally, in opposite directions, so in the pair's equation the two pulls cancel. It is not zero: the trailer's own equation shows it.

optionNotes.option: The tension is zero while they accelerate
optionNotes.why: The tow-bar is pulling hard, as the trailer's own equation shows, and it drops out only of the pair's equation.

optionNotes.option: The trailer is lighter than the car
optionNotes.why: The masses have nothing to do with it: the tow-bar's two pulls are equal and opposite whatever the vehicles weigh.

optionNotes.option: The tension is zero while the bodies accelerate
optionNotes.why: It can feel as if the tension disappears, but it is still in each body's own equation; it only drops out of their sum.

optionNotes.option: The two bodies have equal weights
optionNotes.why: The weights usually differ and that difference drives the motion; what cancels is the tension, one pull helping and one opposing.

caption: The only three the specification allows: both horizontal, both vertical, or one of each.

md: The Teacher Guidance allows exactly three arrangements: **both horizontal** (a car and trailer, with no pulley), **both vertical** (either side of a pulley) and **one of each** (a table and a hanging block). The method is the same in all three; only the forces in each equation change.

stem: An 11 kg block and a 9 kg block are joined by a light inextensible string. Find their acceleration in each of the three arrangements. Take $g = 10$ m/s².

steps.working: Both horizontal, pulled by 60 N: $60 = 20a$, so $a = 3$ m/s²
steps.decision: No pulley and no weight along the motion: the pull drives both masses.
Either side of a pulley, the difference of the weights drives both masses.

steps.working: One of each, the 11 kg on a smooth table: $90 = 20a$, so $a = 4.5$ m/s²
steps.decision: Only the hanging weight drives; the table balances the other block's weight.

prompt: Which arrangement of two connected bodies is NOT set on this specification?
options: Both bodies on an inclined plane, joined over a pulley at the top
Both bodies hanging either side of a pulley
One body on a table, the other hanging over a pulley at the edge
answer: Both bodies on an inclined plane, joined over a pulley at the top
explain: The three rows of See it are the whole list: both horizontal, both vertical, or one of each. A slope with a pulley at the top is an A-level arrangement, and CCEA does not set it.

twin.prompt: Which arrangement of two connected bodies can be set on this specification?
options: A car towing a trailer along a level road
Two blocks on a slope, joined over a pulley at the top
Three blocks joined by two strings
twin.answer: A car towing a trailer along a level road
twin.explain: Both bodies horizontal is one of the three arrangements. Slopes with pulleys and three connected bodies are A-level mechanics.

optionNotes.option: Two blocks on a slope, joined over a pulley at the top
optionNotes.why: Slopes and pulleys together are A-level mechanics; CCEA's pairs are both horizontal, both vertical, or one of each.

optionNotes.option: Three blocks joined by two strings
optionNotes.why: Three or more connected bodies are beyond this specification; the papers only ever join two.

optionNotes.option: Both bodies hanging either side of a pulley
optionNotes.why: This is one of the three arrangements the specification sets: both vertical.

optionNotes.option: One body on a table, the other hanging over a pulley at the edge
optionNotes.why: This is the third arrangement, one of each, and it is the one the papers set most often.

md: Each block has two forces: its weight and $T$. Take each block's own direction of travel as positive, so the heavier block's equation starts with its weight and the lighter block's starts with $T$.

Adding the two equations gives the acceleration; the tension then comes from either block's own equation. Check it in the other one: the tension always lies between the two weights, because one block is being held back and the other lifted.

stem: An 8 kg block and a 2 kg block hang either side of a smooth pulley and are released. Find the acceleration and the tension. Take $g = 10$ m/s².

steps.decision: The heavier block goes down, so its equation starts with its weight.
The lighter block goes up, so its equation starts with the tension.
The tensions cancel; both masses are accelerated.
Back into the 2 kg's equation, then the check in the other: $80 - 32 = 48$, which is $8 \times 6$.

why: Two blocks either side of one pulley, worked against this specification. Before each equation, say which way is positive for that block.

steps.decision: Its weight drives it down and the tension holds it back.

title: FM Pulleys 2 - on smooth table
why: Taught against this specification by name. Watch the two free-body diagrams go down before either equation is written.

prompt: A 6 kg block on a smooth table is joined over a pulley to a 9 kg hanging block. What is their acceleration, in m/s²? Take $g = 10$ m/s².
explain: As in steps 1 to 3 of See it, with no friction because the table is smooth: $90 - T = 9a$ and $T = 6a$ add to $90 = 15a$, so $a = 6$ m/s². The table block brings its mass but no force.

twin.prompt: A 4 kg block on a smooth table is joined over a pulley to a 1 kg hanging block. What is their acceleration, in m/s²? Take $g = 10$ m/s².
twin.explain: $10 - T = 1a$ and $T = 4a$ add to $10 = 5a$, so $a = 2$ m/s².

md: There is no pulley, and both vehicles move the same way. A resistance given per kilogram belongs to one vehicle, so multiply by its own mass. The whole system gives $a$, because the tow-bar's pull is internal and cancels; for the tension, use one vehicle on its own.

stem: A 1100 kg car tows a 300 kg trailer along a level road with a driving force of 3430 N. The resistances are 1.2 N per kg on the car and 0.5 N per kg on the trailer. Find the acceleration and the tension in the tow-bar.

steps.decision: Each per-kilogram resistance uses its own vehicle's mass.
The tow-bar pulls the trailer forwards and the car backwards, so it cancels in the whole.
The tension needs one vehicle on its own, and the trailer has fewer forces.

prompt: A trailer of mass 500 kg is towed with an acceleration of 1.2 m/s² against a resistance of 250 N. What is the tension in the tow-bar, in newtons?
explain: Use the trailer alone, as in step 3 of See it: the tow-bar pulls it forwards and its own resistance holds it back, so $T - 250 = 500 \times 1.2$ and $T = 850$ N. The car's forces never enter the trailer's equation.

md: The string presses on the pulley from both sides. Each section pulls it with force $T$ along that section, so the force on the pulley is the **resultant** of two pulls: their vector sum, not just their sizes added. When both sections hang vertically the pulls point the same way, so the force is $2T$, straight down.

stem: The 8 kg and 2 kg blocks above hang from a string whose tension is 32 N. Find the force the string exerts on the pulley.

steps.working: Each section pulls the pulley down with 32 N
steps.decision: The pulley feels the string, not the blocks: two pulls of $T$, one along each section.

steps.working: Both sections are vertical, so the two pulls point the same way
steps.decision: Parallel pulls add directly.
Twice the tension, and only because the sections are parallel.

explain: Both sections hang vertically, as in step 2 of See it, so the two 26 N pulls point the same way and simply add: 52 N, straight down.

md: When the string runs along a table and over a pulley at its edge, one section is horizontal and the other vertical. Draw both pulls from the axle: equal sides at $90°$ make a square, and the resultant is its diagonal. By Pythagoras, $R^2 = T^2 + T^2$, which is $2T^2$, so $R = T\sqrt{2}$, at $45°$ to each section.

title: Summer 2025, Question 4(iv)
md: The least well-answered part of that paper: a large number of candidates simply doubled the tension. The method mark was for combining the two pulls by Pythagoras, so draw them first.

stem: A string runs along a table and over a pulley at its edge, so one section is horizontal and the other vertical, each with tension $T$. Show that the force on the pulley is $T\sqrt{2}$.

steps.working: Two pulls of size $T$, at $90°$ to each other
steps.decision: Draw both from the axle, one along each section.
Equal sides at a right angle make a square, and the resultant is its diagonal, by Pythagoras.
The square root of $2T^2$; the diagonal of a square halves its corner.

steps.working: For the table pair above, $T = 27.3$ N: $R = 27.3\sqrt{2} = 38.61$ N
steps.decision: Only the tension changes from one question to the next.

prompt: A string runs horizontally along a table, over a pulley at the edge, and vertically down. The tension is 30 N. What is the magnitude of the force on the pulley, in newtons, to 2 decimal places?
explain: Draw the two 30 N pulls from the axle: they make a square, as in step 2 of See it, and the force is its diagonal, $R = 30\sqrt{2} = 42.43$ N. Doubling to 60 N is what a large number of candidates did in Summer 2025.

twin.explain: $R = 17\sqrt{2} = 24.04$ N: the diagonal of the square the two pulls make.

md: When the heavier block lands, the string goes slack: no tension, and the pair's acceleration no longer applies. The lighter block is still rising, now under its weight alone, so with up positive its acceleration is $-10$ m/s², not the old $a$ and not $+10$.

stem: Blocks P (8 kg) and Q (2 kg) hang either side of a smooth pulley, both 0.9 m above the floor, and are released; they accelerate at 6 m/s². P hits the floor. Find the greatest height of Q above the floor. Take $g = 10$ m/s².

steps.decision: Both blocks move 0.9 m together at the pair's acceleration.

steps.working: Q, up positive, under its weight alone: $0 = 10.8 - 2 \times 10 \times s$, so $s = 0.54$ m
steps.decision: No tension now: Q slows at 10 m/s², not at the pair's 6.
Q started 0.9 m up and rose 0.9 m while P fell, then 0.54 m more.

prompt: The lighter of two blocks either side of a pulley is moving upwards at 4 m/s when the heavier one lands and the string goes slack. How much higher does it rise, in metres? Take $g = 10$ m/s².
explain: Only its weight acts now, as in step 2 of See it: with up positive, $0 = 4^2 - 20s$, so $s = 0.8$ m. The pair's acceleration no longer applies.

md: When a tow-bar breaks, the trailer keeps its speed for a moment but loses its pull. Only its resistance acts along the road, so it slows down, while the car, still driving, speeds up. Each needs its own equation from now on.

stem: The 300 kg trailer of the car-and-trailer section is moving at 7 m/s when its tow-bar breaks. Its resistance stays 150 N. Find its deceleration and how far it goes before it stops.

steps.working: No tension now: only the 150 N resistance acts along the road
steps.decision: Redraw the trailer on its own.
Its own resistance over its own mass.
Forwards is positive, so the deceleration enters as a negative acceleration.

prompt: A trailer of mass 500 kg is moving at 8 m/s when its tow-bar breaks. The resistance to its motion is 400 N. What is its deceleration, in m/s²?
explain: With the tow-bar gone only the resistance acts along the road, as in step 2 of See it: $400 = 500a$, so the deceleration is $0.8$ m/s². Its speed decides how far it goes, not how fast it slows.

twin.prompt: A trailer of mass 800 kg is moving at 12 m/s when its tow-bar breaks. The resistance to its motion is 200 N. What is its deceleration, in m/s²?

md: **The connection goes** (2019, 2022, 2024, 2026). A block lands, a string goes slack or a tow-bar breaks: redraw each body on its own, with no tension.
**Resistance per kilogram** (2019, 2024, 2026). Multiply by that vehicle's own mass, never the total.
**The pulley's force** (2022, 2025). A part after the tension asks for it. First line: parallel sections give $2T$; a right angle, $T\sqrt{2}$.
**Kinematics first** (2021, 2023). The pair is timed, or reaches a speed, before any force is given: find $a$ from a constant-acceleration formula first.
**An unknown to show** (2023, 2024, 2026). A mass or a resistance is the unknown, often in a show-that. First line: an equation with the letter in it; the value must come out, not go in.
**A later value, used early** (2024). A value printed in a later part and used in an earlier one scored nothing. Use only what you have been given so far.

stem: A pair of blocks on a table is released from rest and is moving at 3 m/s 1.5 seconds later. Before any force, find the acceleration.

steps.decision: The timing gives the acceleration; no force can be found without it.
Only now do the equations of motion start.

prompt: A part says that 2 seconds after release from rest the blocks are moving at 5 m/s, then asks for the friction on the block on the table. What should the first line be?
options: v = u + at, to find the acceleration
The hanging block's equation of motion
Friction equals the hanging block's weight
answer: v = u + at, to find the acceleration
explain: No force can be found until $a$ is known, and the timing gives it, as step 1 of See it did: $5 = 0 + 2a$, so $a = 2.5$ m/s². Then the hanging block gives $T$, and the table block the friction.

twin.prompt: A part says a hanging block falls 2 m in the first 2 seconds after release from rest, then asks for the tension. What should the first line be?
options: s = ut + ½at², to find the acceleration
The tension equals the hanging block's weight
The table block's equation of motion
twin.answer: s = ut + ½at², to find the acceleration
twin.explain: The distance and the time give $a$ first: $2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times a \times 2^2$, so $a = 1$ m/s². Then the equations of motion.

optionNotes.option: The tension equals the hanging block's weight
optionNotes.why: Only if it hung still; it is accelerating downwards, so its weight is bigger than the tension.

optionNotes.option: The table block's equation of motion
optionNotes.why: It has the tension and the acceleration both unknown; the distance and the time give the acceleration first.

optionNotes.option: The hanging block's equation of motion
optionNotes.why: Its equation still has two unknowns, the tension and the acceleration, so the timing has to give the acceleration first.

optionNotes.option: Friction equals the hanging block's weight
optionNotes.why: That would be true only if nothing moved, but the blocks are speeding up, so the forces do not balance.

text: See it: an unknown to show

stem: A 1400 kg car with a 3500 N driving force tows a trailer of mass $M$ kg at 1.5 m/s². Each vehicle is resisted by 0.5 N per kg. Find the tension in the tow-bar, then $M$.

steps.decision: The car's equation has only $T$ unknown.
Found before $M$ is touched.
The unknown stays a letter until the working produces it.

prompt: A car of known mass tows a trailer of unknown mass M, and a later part asks you to show the value of M. How should you find the tension in the tow-bar first?
options: From the car's own equation
From the trailer's equation, using the M from the later part
From the whole system's equation
explain: The car's equation has only $T$ unknown, which is how step 1 of See it found $T$ before $M$ was touched. The 2024 report found that a value printed in a later part and used earlier scored nothing, and the whole system's equation has no $T$ in it at all.

twin.prompt: A car of unknown mass tows a trailer whose mass, resistance and acceleration are all given. How should you find the tension in the tow-bar first?
options: From the trailer's own equation
From the car's equation, using the car's mass from a later part
From the whole system's equation
twin.explain: Here the trailer's equation is the one with only the tension unknown. Whichever vehicle is fully known gives the tension.

optionNotes.option: From the car's equation, using the car's mass from a later part
optionNotes.why: A value from a later part is not yours to use yet, and here the car's equation has two unknowns anyway.
The tension cancels out of the pair's equation, so it can never give it.

optionNotes.option: From the trailer's equation, using the M from the later part
optionNotes.why: A value printed in a later part may not be used earlier: in Summer 2024 this substitution scored nothing for the whole part.
The tow-bar's pull is internal to the pair, so the whole system's equation has no tension in it at all.

md: The hardest shape so far (2019) lets the car run on after the tow-bar breaks, still driving and still resisted, and asks for its speed later. Here a 1000 kg car tows a 600 kg trailer, each resisted by 0.8 N per kg.

title: Where the specification stops
md: Two bodies joined over a pulley on an inclined plane, three or more connected bodies, and friction written as $F = \mu R$ are A-level mechanics. CCEA's pairs are both horizontal, both vertical, or one of each.

stem: A 1000 kg car tows a 600 kg trailer from rest with a driving force of 3200 N; each is resisted by 0.8 N per kg. The tow-bar breaks after 10 s. Find the car's speed 5 s after the break.

steps.decision: Both vehicles and both resistances, while the bar holds.
The speed carries across the break; the acceleration does not.
Its own driving force, its own resistance, its own mass.
A new stage, starting from the speed at the break.

prompt: After a tow-bar breaks, a car of mass 800 kg keeps its 2500 N driving force and its 500 N resistance. What is its acceleration now, in m/s²?
explain: After the break the car is on its own, as in step 3 of See it: $2500 - 500 = 800a$, so $a = 2.5$ m/s². With no trailer to pull, all of its spare force goes into its own mass.

twin.prompt: After a tow-bar breaks, a car of mass 1200 kg keeps its 3000 N driving force and its 600 N resistance. What is its acceleration now, in m/s²?

md:
Write one equation per body with the same $T$ and $a$, and add them to find $a$.
Find $T$ from one body's own equation; for a tow-bar, from one vehicle's.
Find the force on a pulley: $2T$ for parallel sections, $T\sqrt{2}$ at a right angle.
Start again when the connection goes: no tension, and each body on its own.
Spot the twists: kinematics first, per-kilogram resistance, an unknown to show.

This is one of the long questions, usually Q4, Q5 or Q6: a force diagram for 2 marks, the acceleration, the tension, then the pulley or what happens after the connection goes. Each correct equation of motion earns its own marks, and follow-through runs through every part. Stuck? Write each body's equation, add them, and draw the two pulls before the pulley part.
